keep: The old text held no cure — only a clue about temperature.
lede: She read a fourth-century handbook for what it did not say. The recipe never called for heat.
copy: Project 523 was founded on 23 May 1967 and named for the date. North Vietnam had asked Beijing for help with malaria, which was killing more of its soldiers than the war was; the programme was military, classified, and run straight through the Cultural Revolution, when most Chinese science had stopped. Tu Youyou was put in charge of her institute's group in 1969. Her team worked through hundreds of traditional preparations and kept arriving at the same plant, qinghao — sweet wormwood — and the same failure: extracts that worked in the literature did nothing in mice.

The fix came from a sentence in Ge Hong's 'Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies', written in the fourth century. It said to steep the herb in water and wring out the juice. It did not say to boil it, and almost every other preparation in the tradition does. She took the omission as a fact about chemistry: heat was destroying the compound. Switching to ether, which boils far below water, produced extract number 191, and in October 1971 it inhibited Plasmodium berghei in mice completely (Tu's own account, in Cell, 2011). She and colleagues took the extract themselves before it went near a patient. Clinical trials followed in Hainan in 1972.

She had no doctorate, no medical degree and no training outside China — a combination Chinese coverage of her Nobel returned to so often it acquired a name, the three noes. The Lasker came in 2011, the Nobel in 2015, forty years after the work. The thing the popular retelling flattens is which half was ancient. The text supplied a clue about temperature; everything after that was isolation, structure and dosing, and none of it is in Ge Hong. Artemisinin has been failing since: the WHO's World Malaria Report 2025 confirms partial resistance in Eritrea, Rwanda, Uganda and Tanzania, with four more countries suspected, on top of two decades of it across the Mekong. The compound that saved millions is now on a clock, which is the ordinary fate of drugs and the reason the work is never finished.

bio.t: Tu Youyou and the Discovery of Artemisinin: 2015 Nobel Laureate in Physiology or Medicine
bio.a: Rao Yi, Zhang Daqing and Li Runhong
bio.why: An independent historical account rather than the authorised one Tu wrote herself, which matters for a discovery this contested inside China. There is no popular English biography to correct against, and that absence is itself part of the story.

contested: Whether the credit is hers alone. Project 523 drew in hundreds of researchers across dozens of institutions, and when the Lasker went to Tu by name in 2011 a number of Chinese scientists and institutes argued that a state-run collective programme had been rewritten as one woman's discovery. The Cell paper of the same year reads in part as a formal answer to that objection, which tells you how live it was. The difficulty is that the archive was classified and much of it was never kept in a form that assigns credit to individuals at all — the programme was designed not to. There is no document that would settle who first proposed the ether extraction, and the people who could say are mostly dead.

across.txt: — the other twentieth-century life whose whole output was one compound, and the same argument about whether it merely bought time.
